stem: A cancer survivor tells the nurse, 'I keep blaming myself for choices I made before I got cancer. I feel so guilty that I have stopped talking to my friends about what I am going through.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?

options.A: Acknowledge the guilt without reinforcing self-blame, explore how it is affecting coping and relationships, and offer counseling or support resources if the feelings are persistent or overwhelming.
options.B: Tell the client that guilt is useful because self-blame is necessary to prevent cancer from recurring.
options.C: Avoid discussing the guilt because emotional reactions after cancer treatment have little relevance to survivorship care.
options.D: Explain that withdrawing from friends is the healthiest way to manage guilt until the feeling disappears on its own.

rationale: NCI notes that many people with cancer experience guilt and may blame themselves for lifestyle choices, the burden of treatment on loved ones, costs, missed work, or other concerns. Guilt and self-blame can also occur as part of cancer-related post-traumatic stress and may contribute to withdrawal and impaired coping. The nurse should invite discussion, assess the impact on daily life and relationships, and connect the client with counseling, a support group, or other appropriate psychosocial resources when guilt is difficult to manage. Reinforcing blame or encouraging isolation can worsen distress.
educational_objective: Respond therapeutically to cancer-related guilt and self-blame by assessing its impact on coping and relationships and facilitating appropriate psychosocial support without reinforcing blame or avoidance.
source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health
source_document_title: Emotions and Cancer; Cancer-Related Post-Traumatic Stress
source_locator: Emotions and Cancer — Guilt and emotional support; Cancer-Related Post-Traumatic Stress — guilt/self-blame, avoidance, and treatment/support
source_claim_supported: NCI recognizes guilt and self-blame as psychosocial experiences in people with cancer and cancer survivors, notes that guilt can be associated with withdrawal or post-traumatic stress symptoms, and recommends discussion with the care team, counseling, or support groups when distress is significant.

correction_summary: Rebuilt the original narrowly framed 'survivor guilt because others died' recognition item into an NCI-supported cancer-related guilt and self-blame scenario. The final question requires therapeutic assessment of guilt's impact on relationships and coping plus appropriate support, instead of merely labeling a psychosocial phenomenon. Removed the unsupported implication that one specific survivor-guilt narrative is universal or uniquely defined in oncology.
audit_findings: Original item used a specific survivor-guilt formulation without a strong current source establishing that exact construct as the intended universal survivorship pattern.
Fresh NCI review directly supports guilt, self-blame, social withdrawal, counseling, and support-group referral as relevant cancer psychosocial issues.
The final item moves from terminology recognition to nursing assessment and therapeutic support.
The response neither minimizes the client's feelings nor reinforces causal certainty or moral blame for developing cancer.
Independent adversarial review found one uniquely correct therapeutic response with no ambiguity, second answer, cueing, stigmatizing blame, or unresolved source conflict.
